question:
The figure below is a map showing \(12\) cities and \(17\) roads connecting certain pairs of cities. Paula wishes to travel along exactly \(13\) of those roads, starting at city \(A\) and ending at city \(L,\) without traveling along any portion of a road more than once. (Paula is allowed to visit a city more than once.) How many different routes can Paula take?

[Figure 1](figures/2019_AMC_12B_Q10_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
Paula uses 13 of the 17 roads, so exactly four roads are omitted. Tracking the ends of those omitted roads is easier than listing possible journeys.

[Figure 1](figures/2019_AMC_12B_Q10_question_fig1.svg)

Label the cities from left to right as \(A,B,C,D\) in the top row, \(E,F,G,H\) in the middle row, and \(I,J,K,L\) in the bottom row. A city's degree is the number of roads incident to it.

At every city other than \(A\) and \(L\), the used roads come in arrival-departure pairs, even when Paula visits that city several times. Thus its used degree is even. The used degrees at \(A\) and \(L\) are odd because they are the starting and ending cities.

In the original map, the odd-degree cities are
\[
B,C,E,H,J,K.
\]
The original degrees of \(A\) and \(L\) are even. Therefore the omitted roads must have odd degree at each of
\[
A,B,C,E,H,J,K,L
\]
and even degree at every other city. Four omitted roads have only eight ends altogether. Hence each of these eight cities is incident to exactly one omitted road, and no other city is incident to any omitted road.

This forces all four omissions. Among these eight cities, \(C\) is adjacent only to \(B\), \(E\) only to \(A\), \(H\) only to \(L\), and \(J\) only to \(K\). The omitted roads are therefore
\[
BC,\quad AE,\quad HL,\quad JK.
\]
Every valid route must consequently start along \(A\to B\to F\). Before crossing \(FG\), Paula must traverse the cycle \(F\to E\to I\to J\to F\); otherwise she could never reach its unused roads without repeating \(FG\). She can traverse this cycle in either direction.

After crossing \(FG\), she must likewise traverse \(G\to C\to D\to H\to G\), in either direction, before finishing along \(G\to K\to L\). All roads outside the two cycles are forced. Each pair of cycle directions gives one valid route of length
\[
2+4+1+4+2=13.
\]
Different direction pairs give different routes, and the forced omissions show that every valid route has been included. Thus there are
\[
2\cdot2=\boxed4
\]
routes, choice E.
